title.text: Inference: the type is always declared

phrase.text: In PseudoLearn no variable guesses its type: each one is declared with
and an explicit type before it is used.

runs.text: In PseudoLearn no variable guesses its type: each one is declared with
and an explicit type before it is used.
Some languages deduce the type of a variable from the first value it receives. PseudoLearn does not: the
is required and the type is always written. The initial value is optional and never decides the type.

blocks.description: A Define total As Integer line creates an empty box named total. Below, the assignment total gets 10 stores a value in that box. A note recalls that assigning to an undeclared name is an error.

caption.text: First the box is declared with its shape; then values can be stored. An assignment never creates a new box.

blocks.title: Declare and then assign

runs.text: Assigning to a name nobody declared does not create a variable: it is an error. That way a typo such as
is found before running, instead of silently creating a new variable.

Why does a language designed for learning require declarations? The short answer: a declaration is a promise the engine can check, and typos in variable names are among the hardest mistakes to spot by eye.

points.text: The initial value is optional and does not decide the type.
Assigning to an undeclared name is an error, not a declaration.
